props.title: Requiem for a Vampire

sections.content: Jean Rollin's Requiem for a Vampire represents the peak of French arthouse horror's experimental period. The film's opening 15 minutes unfold without dialogue, following two young women in clown costumes fleeing through a cemetery - establishing Rollin's dreamlike visual approach that influenced later surrealist horror like Suspiria (1977) and The Company of Wolves (1984). The vampire elements serve more as poetic metaphor than traditional horror, similar to how Vampyr (1932) used supernatural elements to explore themes of youth and death.

sections.content: The early 1970s marked a fascinating convergence of exploitation cinema and avant-garde filmmaking, especially in European vampire films. While Hammer was still producing traditional Gothic horror like Vampire Circus (1972), continental directors were pushing boundaries. Blood for Dracula (1974) brought Andy Warhol's factory aesthetic to vampire mythology, while Harry Kümel's Daughters of Darkness (1971) infused vampirism with elegant eroticism and social commentary. SUBHEAD: The French Horror Revolution

Rollin's work emerged alongside other French filmmakers challenging horror conventions. The Iron Rose (1973) and Fascination (1979) continued his poetic approach to horror, while Eyes Without a Face (1960) had earlier established France's ability to blend horror with high art. This movement influenced later French extremity films like High Tension (2003) and Inside (2007), though these took a more visceral approach compared to Rollin's dreamlike atmosphere.
